
  Tonight felt different. The letter sat on his kitchen table, informing him that automation would replace his beloved
  lighthouse keeper's role. In three months, computer systems would manage the light. His hands, weathered by decades of
  rope and metal, would no longer be needed.

  He ascended the stairs slowly, breathing in the familiar scent of oil and salt air. The lamp room greeted him like an
  old friend. Marcus struck the match, watching the great Fresnel lens ignite in its precise, ancient dance. The beam
  swept across the black water in rhythmic circles—a heartbeat keeping the world awake.

  He thought of the ships he'd saved. The cargo vessel in the storm of '89, its radio dead, guided by his light alone.
  The fishing boat with engine failure, drifting toward doom until they saw the lighthouse and knew they were safe. The
  Coast Guard cutter that had radioed him after the incident: "Your light is all that stood between us and the rocks.
  Thank you, keeper."

  How many lives had passed through that beam? How many souls had looked up at this tower and felt the quiet reassurance
  of human vigilance?

  Marcus pulled an old logbook from the shelf, its leather cover cracked with age. Every night recorded—every flame lit,
  every clear sky, every fog so thick you couldn't see your hand before your face. Yet still, he had climbed these
  stairs. Still, he had kept his light burning.

  The wind picked up, rattling the glass windows. Marcus placed his weathered hand on the warm lamp casing, feeling its
  familiar heat beneath his palm. This light had outlived empires, wars, and countless human dramas. It would outlive
  him too.

  He descended the stairs as the beam continued its eternal rotation above, passing through the darkness with patient
  precision. Tomorrow, he would begin training the new system. But tonight, Marcus stood outside and watched his
  lighthouse do what it had always done—reach out into the darkness and say: You are not alone. You are safe. I am still
  here.

  The light swept past him, warm and golden, as it had a thousand nights before.
